test_text.title: Cutty Sark: the fastest sailing ship of all time

article.title: Cutty Sark: the fastest sailing ship of all time

items.sentence_raw: The nineteenth century was a period of great technological development in Britain, and for shipping the major changes were from wind to steam power, and from wood to iron and steel.
The fastest commercial sailing vessels of all time were clippers, three-masted ships built to transport goods around the world, although some also took passengers.
items.explain: Q1: The passage says clippers were *'built to transport goods'*, and *'some also took passengers'* — this means passengers were extra, not the main purpose. The question says they were ***originally intended*** for passengers, which is the opposite. So the answer is **FALSE**.

items.sentence_raw: From the 1840s until 1869, when the Suez Canal opened and steam propulsion was replacing sail, clippers dominated world trade.
Although many were built, only one has survived more or less intact: Cutty Sark, now on display in Greenwich, southeast London.
Cutty Sark's unusual name comes from the poem "Tam O'Shanter" by the Scottish poet Robert Bums.
items.explain: Q2: The passage says the name comes from a *'poem'*, but the question says it is the name of a *'character'* — ***a poem is not a character***. The name actually comes from a *'short nightdress'* in the poem, not a person. So the answer is **FALSE**.

items.sentence_raw: Tam, a farmer, is chased by a witch called Nannie, who is wearing a 'cutty sark' - an old Scottish name for a short nightdress.
The witch is depicted in Cutty Sark's figurehead - the carving of a woman typically at the front of old sailing ships.
In legend, and in Burns's poem, witches cannot cross water, so this was a rather strange choice of name for a ship.
Cutty Sark was built in Dumbarton, Scotland, in 1869, for a shipping company owned by John Willis.
To carry out construction, Willis chose a new shipbuilding firm, Scott & Linton, and ensured that the contract with them put him in a very strong position.
items.explain: Q3: The passage says the contract *'put him in a very strong position'* — **'strong position'** means it **favoured** Willis. The question says the contract **favoured Willis**, which matches exactly. So the answer is **TRUE**.

items.sentence_raw: In the end, the firm was forced out of business, and the ship was finished by a competitor.

Willis's company was active in the tea trade between China and Britain, where speed could bring shipowners both profits and prestige, so Cutty Sark was designed to make the journey more quickly than any other ship.
items.explain: Q4: The passage says Cutty Sark was *'designed to make the journey more quickly than any other ship'* — **'more quickly than any other'** means **the fastest**. The question says Willis wanted it to be the **fastest** tea clipper, which is the same idea. So the answer is **TRUE**.

items.sentence_raw: On her maiden voyage, in 1870, she set sail from London, carrying large amounts of goods to China.
She returned laden with tea, making the journey back to London in four months.
However, Cutty Sark never lived up to the high expectations of her owner, as a result of bad winds and various misfortunes.
On one occasion, in 1872, the ship and a rival clipper, "Thermopylae", left port in China on the same day.
Crossing the Indian Ocean, Cutty Sark gained a lead of over 400 miles, but then her rudder was severely damaged in stormy seas, making her impossible to steer.
The ship's crew had the daunting task of repairing the rudder at sea, and only succeeded at the second attempt.
Cutty Sark reached London a week after "Thermopylae".
items.explain: Q5: The passage says Cutty Sark *'reached London a week after Thermopylae'* — **'after'** means it was slower, not faster. The question says Cutty Sark **beat** Thermopylae, which means it arrived first. These are opposites, so the answer is **FALSE**.

items.sentence_raw: Steam ships posed a growing threat to clippers, as their speed and cargo capacity increased.
In addition, the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869, the same year that Cutty Sark was launched, had a serious impact.

While steam ships could make use of the quick, direct route between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea, the canal was of no use to sailing ships, which needed the much stronger winds of the oceans, and so had to sail a far greater distance.
Steam ships reduced the journey time between Britain and China by approximately two months.
items.explain: Q6: The passage says steam ships *'reduced the journey time between Britain and China by approximately two months'* — **'reduced journey time'** means they were **faster**. The question says steam ships could travel **faster** than clippers, which matches. So the answer is **TRUE**.

items.sentence_raw: By 1878, tea traders weren't interested in Cutty Sark, and instead, she took on the much less prestigious work of carrying any cargo between any two ports in the world.
In 1880, violence aboard the ship led ultimately to the replacement of the captain with an incompetent drunkard who stole the crew's wages.
He was suspended from service, and a new captain appointed.
This marked a turnaround and the beginning of the most successful period in Cutty Sark's working life, transporting wool from Australia to Britain.
items.explain: Q9: The passage says the most successful period involved *'transporting wool from Australia to Britain'* — **'transporting'** means it was the main **cargo**. So the answer is **wool**.

items.sentence_raw: One such journey took just under 12 weeks, beating every other ship sailing that year by around a month.
The ship's next captain, Richard Woodget, was an excellent navigator, who got the best out of both his ship and his crew.
items.explain: Q10: The passage says Woodget was *'an excellent navigator'* — **'excellent'** means he was very **skilled**. The question asks for his role besides captain, and **'navigator'** is that role. So the answer is **navigator**.

items.sentence_raw: As a sailing ship, Cutty Sark depended on the strong trade winds of the southern hemisphere, and Woodget took her further south than any previous captain, bringing her dangerously close to icebergs off the southern tip of South America.
items.explain: Q8: The passage says Woodget brought the ship *'dangerously close to icebergs'* — **'dangerously close'** means there was a **risk of hitting** one. The question says he put it **at risk of hitting an iceberg**, which is the same idea. So the answer is **TRUE**.

items.sentence_raw: His gamble paid off, though, and the ship was the fastest vessel in the wool trade for ten years.
As competition from steam ships increased in the 1890s, and Cutty Sark approached the end of her life expectancy, she became less profitable.
She was sold to a Portuguese firm, which renamed her "Ferreira".
For the next 25 years, she again carried miscellaneous cargoes around the world.
Badly damaged in a gale in 1922, she was put into Falmouth harbour in southwest England, for repairs.
items.explain: Q11: The passage says the ship was *'badly damaged in a gale'* and then went to Falmouth for repairs — **'gale'** is a strong storm that caused the damage. So the answer is **gale**.

items.sentence_raw: Wilfred Dowman, a retired sea captain who owned a training vessel, recognised her and tried to buy her, but without success.
She returned to Portugal and was sold to another Portuguese company.
Dowman was determined, however, and offered a high price: this was accepted, and the ship returned to Falmouth the following year and had her original name restored.
Dowman used Cutty Sark as a training ship, and she continued in this role after his death.
items.explain: Q12: The passage says Dowman *'used Cutty Sark as a training ship'* and this continued until 1954 — **'used as'** means its purpose was **training**. So the answer is **training**.

items.sentence_raw: When she was no longer required, in 1954, she was transferred to dry dock at Greenwich to go on public display.
The ship suffered from fire in 2007, and again, less seriously, in 2014, but now Cutty Sark attracts a quarter of a million visitors a year.
items.explain: Q13: The passage says the ship *'suffered from fire in 2007, and again... in 2014'* — **'suffered from'** means it was **damaged by** fire twice. So the answer is **fire**.

orphan_explain_map.7: Q7: The passage says steam ships used the *'quick, direct route'* through the Suez Canal, and sailing ships needed the *'ocean'* route. But the passage never says if steam ships ***sometimes*** used the ocean route too. ***NOT GIVEN is not the same as FALSE*** — so the answer is **NOT GIVEN**.
